ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The attached diagram shows two white upright squares resting on the same horizontal baseline. The left white square is labeled 9, and the right white square is labeled 4. A larger pink square is tilted between them. One lower vertex of the pink square lies on the baseline, its upper-left adjacent vertex touches the top-right corner of the square labeled 9, and its lower-right adjacent vertex touches the top-left corner of the square labeled 4. Reasoning: The numbers 9 and 4 are the areas of the smaller squares, so their side lengths are sqrt(9)=3 and sqrt(4)=2. Put the pink square's lower baseline vertex at the origin. The side from this vertex to the contact point on the 4-square reaches height 2, so write that side vector as (x, 2). The adjacent side from the same vertex to the contact point on the 9-square is perpendicular and has the same length, so it can be represented as a 90-degree rotation, (-2, x). That contact point is at the top-right corner of the 9-square, which is height 3 above the baseline. Therefore x=3. The side length squared of the pink square is x^2+2^2=3^2+2^2=13. Since the area of a square equals its side length squared, the largest square has area 13.

From the text, the labels 9 and 4 are areas, so the small square side lengths are 3 and 2. Put the baseline vertex of the pink square at the origin. The side from this vertex to the contact with the 4-square rises 2 units, so write that side vector as (x, 2). The adjacent side to the contact with the 9-square is a perpendicular equal-length side, so it is a 90-degree rotation of this vector, e.g. (-2, x). Since that contact point is at height 3 above the baseline, x = 3. Therefore the pink square side length squared is x^2 + 2^2 = 3^2 + 2^2 = 13, which is its area.
